articles.title: Watch: US journalist Evan Gershkovich describes being detained by Russian agents
articles.summary: He was arrested in Russia in 2023 and later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges.

blocks.text: US journalist Evan Gershkovich has told the BBC's Today programme about the 16 months when he was detained in Russia.

In his first UK broadcast interview, the Wall Street Journal correspondent said he realised he had been "lured into a trap" when masked men surrounded him at a restaurant in March 2023, and arrested him.
He was later sentenced to 16 years on espionage charges, but released in 2024 as part of a high-profile prisoner exchange.
He and his employer have always maintained that the charges were false, and following his arrest, then-US President Joe Biden said he had "no higher priority" than bringing Gershkovich home.

articles.title: RFK Jr outlines expansive vision for collecting US health data at Maha event
articles.summary: Health secretary calls for medical and lifestyle details to be sent to doctors and AI to address ‘chronic disease epidemic’

blocks.text: Robert F Kennedy Jr laid out an expansive vision for collecting, sharing and analyzing US health information at a Maha event hosted by a close ally and outspoken anti-vaccine activist.

Medical and lifestyle data, from doctor’s visits to exercise, should be connected and shared with the government and independent researchers, where it can be searched by AI – including potential links between vaccines and health outcomes including autism and mortality, suggested Kennedy, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine skeptic.

“We need to use America’s health data to determine whether the food we eat, the chemicals we encounter, the vaccines that we’re administering, the other environmental and lifestyle exposures are contributing in one way or another to the chronic disease epidemic,” Kennedy said at an event with the Maha Institute on Monday, with about two dozen people tuning into the live stream.

The Maha Institute is headed by Mark Gorton, who called himself “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference” two weeks ago. The institute was co-founded by Tony Lyons, whose publishing house gave $4m to Kennedy through various Maha foundations with funding from political contributions and health-related corporations, according to reporting by the New York Times.

Kennedy has focused on pulling together data from all of the agencies he oversees, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS).

”Your health information should follow you wherever you go,” Kennedy said. Providers, insurance and technology companies are creating apps for portable health records, for instance – making it easier for individuals to access their medical records, and also opening up the records for governmental and outside use.

“Medicaid is a really useful vehicle for studying that because there are hundreds of millions of lives in there, including tens of millions of children who’ve been in that program for 10 or 20 years,” Kennedy said. The Trump administration is now tracking “exposures”, interventions and claim data in Medicaid, and “Medicare gives us enormous amounts of information on older Americans and people with disabilities,” he said.

FDA monitoring systems can link claims data and electronic health records “to conduct active safety surveillance”, while commercial platforms, such as HealthVerity, can link insurance claims, prescriptions, laboratory results and electronic health records, he said.

State-level datasets reported to the CDC are “unusable” because they often collect different data points, Kennedy said: “Too many of those systems remain siloed and cannot give us the real-time information we need to understand health at scale.” Yet wider access to state health data could allow officials and others to connect immunization records, clinical data, laboratory results, pharmacy information and insurance claims “to create a more complete picture of a patient’s health over a long period of time”, Kennedy said.

Federal officials are using AI to process the data, he said: “Studies that used to take years, you can do them literally in seconds. You can ask questions and you can get immediate answers, and that’s what we’re doing today.”

Kennedy repeatedly touted the benefits of AI, which has been embraced by some in the anti-vaccine world for purportedly showing the dangers of vaccines. “It can help researchers find patterns across millions of health histories that human beings could never find by reading those records one at a time,” Kennedy said.

OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman met with Kennedy this week and told him that HHS uses generative AI – Kennedy used the term “superintelligence” – more than any other federal agency, Kennedy said. OpenAI agents hacked US government websites and the Australian Medicare website this summer, reporting recently revealed.

“We’re already using all of these data to answer some of our most important questions,” Kennedy said. Officials have created an autism registry despite widespread protest. The Trump administration has also launched studies on the roles of such factors as diet, electromagnetic fields, screen time and vaccines in the development of illness, Kennedy said.

He repeatedly returned to vaccines. At the CDC, officials are using the Vaccine Safety Datalink (VSD) to compare outcomes in healthcare for vaccinated and unvaccinated people, as well as examining the role of aluminum adjuvants in vaccines; the timing of the hepatitis B vaccine in infancy; comparing live and attenuated vaccines; and studying influenza, Covid and HPV vaccines in children, Kennedy said.

Using Medicaid and “linked real-world data”, officials are also studying vaccination during pregnancy and subsequent childhood outcomes. FDA researchers are using the Biologics Effectiveness and Safety (Best) System and Medicare data to “replicate and expand previous studies” on vaccinated and unvaccinated populations, aluminum and asthma, and maternal influenza vaccines and autism spectrum disorder, he said.
after newsletter promotion
“We will have answers soon,” Kennedy said. “A more connected health data system will make this research even stronger.”

Kennedy returned repeatedly to an old grievance – how independent citizens attempting to link vaccines to autism were blocked from accessing VSD data in the early 2000s after they violated confidentiality agreements. Mark and David Geier weren’t affiliated with any research institutions at the time of their suspension, and they created their own institutional review board to oversee their work, according to the Maryland state board of physicians, which suspended Mark Geier’s medical license. The board also charged David Geier with practicing medicine without a licence.

“I cannot get access to that data today. I cannot get access to it,” Kennedy said of the VSD data after 2002, which is safeguarded by healthcare organizations for health privacy reasons. “A qualified researcher with a legitimate hypothesis should not need permission from a gatekeeper to test it,” Kennedy said, calling the VSD an “unworkable system”. The Trump administration’s goal now is to make health data “research ready, and then give access to hundreds of external researchers to actually come in and look at it”, Kennedy said.

Gorton, the Maha Institute president, focused on open data in his comments at the event on Monday. But less than two weeks earlier, at a meeting of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, Gorton called vaccines a “public health nightmare”, spread misinformation about their ingredients, claimed that 40% of all kids are “injured” by vaccines because of allergy, asthma and eczema diagnoses, and railed against “the poisoners running the medical system”.

The success of vaccination, frequently called one of the greatest achievements in science, is a “complete fabrication” and “massive fraud”, Gorton said at the 17 September conference. He took particular aim at polio vaccines, claiming that an outbreak of polio in the 1950s was actually because of pesticides. “The supposed success of the polio vaccine was a massive medical fraud and a masterful PR deception,” Gorton claimed.

“The time has come to stop caveating every introduction with ‘I’m not an anti-vaxxer, but …’ Vaccines are a nightmare, and only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough,” Gorton said at that conference, adding: “More vaccines, more autism. It’s that simple.”

Focusing on opening up health data is new for the Maha Institute. But having greater access to US health information would help advocates make new links to the issues they have long focused on, Gorton said on Monday. Organizations including the Maha Institute, which exists outside the government but enjoys close ties to top leaders such as Kennedy, can “fill the gaps” and “bring political pressure”, he said.
Kennedy thanked Gorton, his longtime friend, for his “incredible support”.

articles.title: Berlin Marathon winner limped to finish line after rupturing Achilles tendon chasing world mark
articles.summary: Berlin Marathon winner Tigst Assefa of Ethiopia "completely destroyed" her right Achilles tendon trying to regain her world record.

image.caption: Tigst Assefa of Ethiopia collapsed after crossing the line first in the women's race of the Berlin Marathon on Sunday. She was flown to Munich before undergoing a 'very complex surgery' on her ankle, according to her representative Gianni Demadonna. (John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: New
Berlin Marathon winner Tigst Assefa of Ethiopia "completely destroyed" her right Achilles tendon trying to regain her world record.
Ethiopia's Tigst Assefa posted third fastest women's 42.2 km time ever on Sunday
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 10:35 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Berlin Marathon winner Tigst Assefa "completely destroyed" her right Achilles tendon trying to regain her world record.

Assefa was on well on course to beat Ruth Chepng'etich's world record with two kilometres remaining in Sunday's race when she suddenly began limping with what appeared to be cramps. She grimaced and kept running in visible pain before ultimately finishing 68 seconds behind Chepng'etich's mark of two hours nine minutes 56 seconds from Chicago in 2024.
It transpired she Assefa suffered a "complete rupture of the right Achilles tendon," her representative Gianni Demadonna told The Associated Press on Tuesday.
Demadonna said the Ethiopian runner had been in pain from the 31st kilometre but decided to continue running before the injury struck at the 40K mark.

"She was no longer able to run, because when she was going to put her foot on the ground she had no power," Demadonna said of the issue at the 40 km mark. "She completely destroyed the tendon at the end, because running without the tendon — I mean the last 500 metres maybe she ran without the tendon, you know, only with the heel, so that was a disaster because maybe [if] she had stopped, [it] was not so bad, but she ran two kilometres with the problem."

The 29-year-old Assefa still ran the third fastest time ever in 2:11:04. It's her third victory in Berlin after 2022 and 2023, but she had been pushing for another world record after her record time of 2:11:53 in 2023.
Chepng'etich lowered that mark by nearly two minutes the following year but was banned for three years in 2025 after admitting a doping violation. The Kenyan runner's record still stands.
Assefa was on course to smash Chepng'etich's record on Sunday.
"She was on to run 2:09:30, 2:09:40, so that was the goal, and she still had eight minutes [to run] the last 2.2 kilometers. That is amazing," Demadonna said.

items: In 2023, Assefa shatters women's world record by over 2 minutes in Berlin
Ruth Chepng'etich smashes women's marathon world record in 2025

blocks.text: Assefa collapsed after crossing the line and was attended to by a medic as well as compatriot and marathon great Haile Gebrselassie, among others. She skipped the post-race formalities and was flown to Munich before undergoing what Demadonna called "very complex surgery" on her ankle on Monday at a hospital in Murnau, a town near the Austrian border southwest of Munich.

Demadonna, who was on his way back home to Italy after leaving Assefa in the hospital, said she will see another doctor in Munich on Thursday to see how the surgery went and to start her rehabilitation. He said she will need to use crutches for around six weeks by which time she will have started exercises for movement of the tendon.

"After starting walking and bicycle, maybe [she can] start running in three months, so I think seven months to compete in another marathon, maybe London Marathon 2027 at the end of April, but difficult to say now," Demadonna said. "We have to stay patient and see what the doctor will say."
He added that Assefa "is very sad, but what can we do? She knows that it's a long way to recover but the doctor said, ‘Don't worry, you can recover.' So we will see."

articles.title: US senator blocks bill to ban Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center without Congress’s approval
articles.summary: Mike Lee objected to the safeguard against the demolition of any presidential memorial Congress designates

blocks.text: A Republican senator has blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Donald Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress.

Mike Lee, of Utah, objected on Monday night when Oregon Democrat Jeff Merkley asked the Senate to pass the Protecting Presidential Memorials Act by unanimous consent. The bill, co-written with Alaska Republican Lisa Murkowski, would have banned the demolition of any presidential memorial designated by Congress, including the Lincoln and Jefferson memorials, unless lawmakers explicitly approved it.

“First, he destroyed its programming, and now, he wants to destroy the building itself,” Merkley wrote in a statement. “All because the law says Trump can’t put his name on the building.” He called the president’s threats “straight out of the authoritarian playbook”.

Murkowski, who chairs the appropriations subcommittee that funds the center, said last week that lawmakers had authorized and funded substantial renovation work, but “what was not authorized is a demolition of the Kennedy Center”.

The fight over the Kennedy Center has been one of the longest legal drama’s of Trump’s second term. It started when the president seized control of the center shortly after returning to office, clearing out the board and installing allies while attacking what he called “woke” programming.

Trump’s handpicked board voted last December to rename the venue the Trump-Kennedy Center, but in May, federal judge Christopher Cooper ruled the change illegal and halted a planned two-year closure. On 15 September, Cooper rejected a second attempt to put Trump’s name on the building, and Trump said the $257m renovation would not go ahead unless the decision was reversed.

In August, justice department lawyers warned in court that the building could decay until it had to come down, and floated an outdoor amphitheater as a replacement. A judge has since ordered 30 days’ notice of any demolition plans, and the center’s leader has told the court the building will stay standing.

Lee has been closely aligned with Trump since 2020, and supported his efforts to overturn that year’s election result. More recently, he has repeatedly brought the Trump-backed Save act, which would impose voter ID and citizenship-proof requirements, to the Senate floor, and in April urged Trump to force lawmakers back to Washington to end a partial shutdown and pass it.

Senate Social Media Unit
Impeachment court Reginald Tongol explains the suspension was due to the trial being 'aggressively ahead of schedule'
MANILA, Philippines– The Senate impeachment court has suspended the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte slated for Wednesday, September 30.
The Senate Clerk of Court announced this in a notice dated September 29, and also said that the trial will resume on Thursday, October 1, at 10 am.
Impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said the postponement was not due to delays, but because the trial was “aggressively ahead of schedule.”

“Tomorrow is a deliberate Strategic Procedural Pause designed to clear the floor so both panels can prepare for the grueling, whole-day marathon sessions running continuously from October 1 to 15,” Tongol said in a press statement.

“This pause gives all parties the critical breathing room needed to digest the highly technical, voluminous financial records incoming from the Anti-Money Laundering Council and the Registers of Deeds starting this Thursday,” he said.
Former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV is also expected to be presented as prosecution witness on October 1, the first implementation of the whole-day trial. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson attack on drone maker supplying Ukraine
articles.summary: European and Nato leaders express support for Estonia after August attack on manufacturer in Tallinn
articles.byline: Jon Henley Europe correspondent and agencies

blocks.text: European and Nato leaders have expressed full support for Estonia and Ukraine after the Baltic state said an August arson attack on a drone manufacturer supplying Kyiv was an act of sabotage commissioned by Moscow’s security services.

Estonia’s foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, said on social media on Tuesday that such attacks were “absolutely unacceptable” and that Russia’s chargé d’affaires in the Estonian capital, Tallinn, was being summoned to his ministry.

Estonia’s national security agency said a fire broke out on 15 August at a building in Tallinn used by Milrem Robotics, which makes unmanned ground vehicles used in Ukraine. Two Latvian suspects were detained in Latvia on 17 August, followed by a third the next day. All three were handed over to Estonia, it said.

Tsahkna said the subsequent investigation had led authorities to “conclude with certainty” that the attack was “an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation”. It was part of a “broader campaign across Europe aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine”, he said.

Estonia’s prime minister, Kristen Michal, said his country’s response to Russia’s campaign would “be the opposite: stronger security at home, more support for Ukraine and greater pressure on Russia. We will not be intimidated.”

Estonia has repeatedly accused Russia of hybrid provocations since the beginning of Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and, along with its fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, has significantly increased its defence spending.

Dmitry Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Estonia’s allegations were “unfounded, ill-considered, absolutely not reflecting the reality, not containing any substantiation whatsoever”. He said Russia “cannot take such statements seriously, and we won’t”.

Western allies pledged their continued support to Estonia and Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels, Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said Russia “continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies”, adding that it was “failing … on the battlefield in Ukraine, and failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine”.

Speaking alongside Rutte, Lithuania’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said Russia’s actions were becoming “increasingly hostile and less restrained … We see the hybrid attacks – in Lithuania, Poland, Germany, elsewhere. And it’s not a question of proximity now, it’s a question of Russia’s actions.”
after newsletter promotion

Lithuania’s foreign minister, Kęstutis Budrys, said Russia’s fingerprints were “all over” the Tallinn attack, while the Latvian president, Edgars Rinkēvičs, said further support for Ukraine “will be needed, and must be provided”.

The EU said it stood with Estonia, describing the arson attack as “reckless” and saying it would not be put off supporting Ukraine. “Moscow is trying to scare Europe into winding down its support for Ukraine. This will not happen,” a European Commission spokesperson said.

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron, called the arson attack a “dangerous escalation”. Moscow “needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine”, Macron said on social media.

Sweden’s acting prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called Estonia’s formal attribution of the attack “extremely serious”, and Britain’s ambassador to Estonia, Jo Lomas, said the UK “stands with Estonia in confronting these unacceptable attacks. They will not weaken our resolve or our support for Ukraine.”

About 200 incidents of suspected Russian sabotage and malign activity have been recorded across Europe since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, including arson plots at warehouses, drone incursions, thefts of defence technology and cyber-attacks on essential European infrastructure.
Agence France-Presse and Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: Satirist launches site naming Cornell students accused in gang-rape lawsuit
articles.summary: Writer Toby Morton is using a new website to amplify allegations in a high-profile sexual assault lawsuit involving seven Cornell students. The reopening of the case is causing an outcry on social…

image.caption: The Chi Phi fraternity was barred from campus in 2024Image: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Toby Morton, who wrote several episodes of the animated comedy series "South Park," launched a website seeking accountability in connection with an alleged 2024 sexual assault case involving seven Cornell University fraternity members. The site names seven men accused of sexually assaulting a 20-year-old woman who was allegedly unconscious after being given drugs and alcohol at a Cornell fraternity house and collects personal data and photos of the members involved.

"I've received messages reminding me I'm not a journalist, I'm 'just a satirist,'" Morton wrote in a September 27 Instagram post regarding the creation of his website TheCornell7.org. "This is true, but it makes me more dangerous," he added, saying he has "nobody to tell me I've gone too far."

The case has recently drawn a surge in public attention after the accuser, identified as Jane Doe to protect her identity, filed a lawsuit in mid-September. Her complaint alleges that she was brutally sexually assaulted in 2024 by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity while unconscious after being pressured to take ketamine, smoke marijuana and drink alcohol at the fraternity house on Cornell's campus in Ithaca, New York. The university, she said in the lawsuit, failed to protect her. Cornell conducted an internal investigation after the incident, but no one was charged.

blocks.caption: The reopening of the case has caused renewed attention on social mediaImage: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Since the lawsuit was filed on September 16, the case has generated widespread commentary on social media. Some have criticized Cornell and the district attorney's office, while others have questioned the allegations.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who handled the original case, said his office has reopened it and plans to present evidence to a grand jury amid public questions about why no criminal charges were initially filed.

Van Houten said in a statement that his office is considering bringing criminal charges related to the incident, though the allegations in the civil complaint are "dramatically different" from the woman's statement to police two years ago — in her statement to authorities, she did not allege she was drugged without her knowledge or that she did not consent to engage in sexual acts.
Justice sought
Cornell's Chi Phi chapter was barred from campus after the alleged incident in 2024. The accuser also dropped out of Cornell University, according to her attorney.

One of the most chilling allegations of the lawsuit is that a message was sent to a Chi Phi Snapchat group at about 1:42 a.m., inviting members to the room to abuse Doe, who was heavily under the influence of drugs and alcohol. The lawsuit alleges that more men then entered the room and that the assault continued for several hours until Doe lost consciousness.

"There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn't. I've never seen anything like it," an attorney for Jane Doe, Thomas Giuffra, told CBS. Giuffra pointed out that two of the seven accused fraternity members were expelled, while the others received lesser disciplinary measures. "Not one of these guys was arrested," Giuffra told the network.

blocks.caption: Actress Florence Pugh described the allegations as 'horrific' on social mediaImage: Cover Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Politicians and actors speak out

Many people, from US politicians to Hollywood actors, have spoken out about the case in recent days. US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a New York Democrat, condemned what she described as a "culture of rape" protected by elite institutions. "When I read what happened at Cornell, those men posted in a group chat. That means it was normal to them. That means it was acceptable to them. This is a culture, and what we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore," she said Sunday at a forum near Cornell's campus.

British actress Florence Pugh described the allegations as "horrific" on social media and expressed her support for the student involved. Pugh, who is also currently on a promotional tour for her upcoming Netflix series "East of Eden," wrote a lengthy statement on Instagram, saying that "Colleges/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world. You build men that get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and that they won't be harmed in return."
"Those who protect and impose light sentences on men who rape and destroy lives should be punished and closely scrutinized. Why are you protecting someone so fiercely?" she wrote.

American actor Josh Gad, best known as the voice of Olaf in Disney's"Frozen" films, also commented on the Cornell case, criticizing what he described as insufficient disciplinary consequences for the students accused of sexual assault. In an Instagram post, Gad said sexual violence should not be treated as a mistake or addressed with limited disciplinary action by a university, arguing that the alleged conduct had "destroyed a life” and calling for greater accountability.
Edited by Joshua Lang.

articles.title: Should Baste Duterte get a free pass for ‘missing’ VP Sara’s ties to Gencorp?
articles.summary: Senator-judge Bong Go defends the Davao City mayor's decision to delegate signing powers, saying the younger Duterte is not the one on trial

blocks.text: While some grilled Davao City Mayor Sebastian “Baste” Duterte over his decision to delegate procurement responsibilities — his defense for supposedly not knowing anything about the his city govenment’s deals with Gencorp Industries Inc. — other senator-judges came in his defense, citing the sheer volume of work mayors handle.
Duterte took the witness stand on Tuesday, September 29, for the impeachment trial of his older sister, Vice President Sara Duterte.

In his testimony, the mayor distanced himself from the Davao City government’s deals with Gencorp, maintaining he had no direct hand in the contracts sealed with the company linked to the Vice President.

The younger Duterte claimed he did not personally review Gencorp’s contracts and did not personally approve such deals because he did not interfere in the undertakings of city hall’s bids and awards committee. He also said he delegated his procurement responsibilities to Davao City Assistant City Administrator Tristan Domingo because of his workload as mayor.
Senator-judge Christopher Lawrence “Bong” Go, in a rare manifestation, defended this decision, citing the voluminous documents the Davao City mayor needed to review and sign.
“Mayor Baste Duterte is not the one on trial here,” said Go.

“I am a witness to the work in the city hall. Davao City is a huge city, and a mayor has a lot of documents to sign. It is impossible for him to go over each document, so he really needed to delegate the task,” he said. Go had served as aide to Duterte’s father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, for four of his seven terms as Davao City mayor.
Senator-judges Alan Peter Cayetano and Joel Villanueva expressed similar remarks, noting the younger Duterte may have to sign at least 2,500 to 3,000 documents a week.

“The point I want to make is this: You will not have any other time to govern if you’re going to have to look at each and every company, each and every document, each and every person…. Under the law, you can rely on the signature of your personnel officer,” Cayetano said.
Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, for his part, asked the mayor if he was advised on the Arias doctrine, as it contained a similar legal principle.

“I asked if you were advised on the Arias doctrine because it lays out the rule that heads of offices are permitted to rely, on good faith, on their subordinates for their action, processing, recommendations,” Lacson said.
Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo urged Mayor Duterte to investigate the city staff and administrator who allowed the contracts between Gencorp and the city government.
Mayor Duterte, however, dismissed Tulfo’s manifestation, saying, “as long as my sister’s name, the Vice President’s name, was not on the contract, then there’s nothing.”

blocks.caption: Sara Duterte’s company won millions’ worth of contracts from Davao City Hall

blocks.text: Outside the courtroom, the prosecution spokespersons said they found the mayor’s insistence that he knew nothing about the Gencorp deals, and that these were aboveboard, difficult to believe.
Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV also offered a contrasting view, warning of the implications of allowing mayors to rely entirely on delegated authority when transactions involve their relatives.

Trillanes, who attended the trial in case he would be called as a prosecution witness on the explained wealth case against the Vice President, was initially hesitant to respond to reporters’ questions in a chance interview during a break in the trial.

When pressed to comment on Mayor Baste’s appearance at the trial, Trillanes finally said: “Siguro heto lang. I’ll give you this. Kung puwede ‘yung sinasabi niya, lahat ng mayor sa Pilipinas puwedeng makipagkontrata sa kapatid nila. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. ‘Yun ang implication dito.“

(Okay, it’s like this. I’ll give you this. If what he says is allowed, all the mayors in the Philippines can sign contracts with their siblings. They will just feign ignorance. So think about that. That’s the implication here.)

image.caption: Senegal have refurbished some of their existing facilities rather than just building new onesImage: Cem Özdel/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal.
Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year.

"We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame.

The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning. It appears that 16 years on since the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, global sport is finally returning to different parts of Africa.
"This is a victory for Africa. It opens the door for Africa to host major events," Malick Diouf, head of a marketing agency and founder of the Dakar Sport Summit, told DW.
"Africa is in the process of opening up to the world, hosting major events and everything. And all of Africa must celebrate this kind of victory."

blocks.caption: Malick Diouf believes Africa as an Olympic host is the logical next stepImage: DW

blocks.text: With more major events in Africa, the question around an Olympic Games being on the continent looms.
Sports scientist Kamilla Swart has said awarding Africa a Games would make the world "take Africa more seriously." Diouf believes it's the logical next step.
"The Youth Olympic Games, it's a major test for Africa. And I think this is where we need to succeed in organizing these Games and also in sending a message," Diouf said.

"We, Africa, are ready to host the Summer Olympics, and I think that would be the logical next step after the Dakar Olympics. We have Olympic champions; we have record holders; we have Olympians, so we deserve to host the Olympic Games."
Senegal an attractive option for many reasons
The move to re-use and refurbish existing facilities rather than build whole new ones is likely why Senegal's bid was so tempting for the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

The fear of the white elephant facility appears to have been considered here. The Iba Mar Diop Stadium, the track and field stadium, is expected to be used for athlete training ahead of the 2028 Olympics.

"It’s by using these facilities, by participating in and hosting international events, and by consistently maintaining them to the required standards, that we’ll be able to keep these stadiums up to the standards they currently meet," Diouf said.

There's also the social and economical impacts of the Youth Olympics. Diouf believes the impact is beyond just infrastructure, but into roads, the development of the hospitality, security and broadcasting sectors and the young athletes themselves.
"There's life after the Games. Now we need to figure out how to use the resources we have, we need to develop and capitalize on what we have showcased during the Games," said Diouf.
Future of Youth Olympics in doubt

The significance of these Games stretch beyond even the history they are making in Africa. In May of this year, IOC President Kirsty Coventry put the brakes on the future of the Youth Olympics, leaving real doubts as to whether there will be any more after the 2028 winter edition.

"We need to pause and have a real reflection on why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games and we realized that across the Movement it's very disjointed. There's not a true North Star of why we're doing the Youth Olympic Games," Coventry told reporters.
"So the EB (IOC Executive Board) decided to pause the 2030 process right now so there will not be an election in June, and rather we need to take a step back and develop a youth strategy."

blocks.caption: The Youth Olympics in Dakar might well be the last summer edition of the youth games, adding even more importance to the first ones in AfricaImage: Nicolas Remene/Le Pictorium/IMAGO

blocks.text: A lot has changed since the Youth Olympic Games were launched in 2010. Initially it was seen as a way to engage a younger audience (athletes were limited by age to between 15 and 18) by trialing new sports as well as testing host country's on a smaller stage. However, with the age of athletes decreasing and the challenges of engaging a younger audience in the modern sports entertainment landscape even more challenging, it appears clear the IOC are reconsidering their options when it comes to investment.
"My only wish is that Dakar be memorable and that people reconsider their decision not to host the Games in 2030," Diouf said.

"I don’t want these to be the last Youth Olympic Games, but if these are to be the last Youth Olympic Games, we need to go out with a bang. Dakar needs to show the world what Senegal is all about, what Africa is all about."
From October 31 to November 13 this year, Senegal will have the chance to do just that.

articles.title: Senate impeachment court cancels hearing on Wednesday for 'strategic pause'
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court canceled the trial session on Wednesday to take a “strategic procedural pause,” according to the tribunal"s spokesperson on Tuesday night.

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 10:03pm
The Senate impeachment court canceled the trial session on Wednesday to take a “strategic procedural pause,” according to the tribunal’s spokesperson on Tuesday night.
The Senate released a notice informing the public that the session for Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, set for September 30, was cancelled and will continue on Thursday, October 1.
In a statement shortly after, Senate impeachment court spokesperson Attorney Regie Tongol clarified that this was not because of a delay.

“The Impeachment Court is not pausing because it is behind; it is pausing because the Court is aggressively ahead of schedule. Since opening Article II on September 14, the proceedings have advanced at a rigorous pace, with the prosecution already presenting six witnesses in an eight-day span that demonstrates a clear commitment to moving the trial forward without unnecessary stalling through highly focused presentation of evidence,” Tongol said in a statement.

“Tomorrow is a deliberate Strategic Procedural Pause designed to clear the floor so both panels can prepare for the grueling, whole-day (10:00 AM to 6:30 PM) marathon sessions running continuously from October 1 to 15,” he added.
The whole-day trial on Thursday will begin at 10:00 a.m., the spokesperson said.

Tongol said that the pause gave all parties critical breathing room as the next set of evidence to be tackled is the “highly technical, voluminous financial records” from the Anti-Money Laundering Council. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Spanish government approves measures to ease housing crisis after outcry over eviction
articles.summary:
Decrees include extending ban on evictions of vulnerable people after 87-year-old was forced out of her home

Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of…

blocks.text: Spain’s Socialist Workers’ party-led coalition government has approved a range of measures aimed at easing the country’s housing crisis, including extending a ban on evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, after a public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old disabled woman from her Madrid apartment last week.

Two decrees have been approved by cabinet but will need to be approved in Congress, where the coalition lacks a majority. The government has requested a special parliamentary session on Friday in the hope of getting the decrees passed as soon as possible.

Although the fine print has yet be revealed, the main decree includes: extending restrictions on evictions of vulnerable tenants to 2030; regulating temporary lettings and lettings by room; a ban on so-called vulture funds buying property until 2028, plus a two-year extension on current rental agreements that are due to expire at the end of 2028.
A separate agreement was reached on the automatic renovation of rental agreements.

blocks.caption: Maricarmen Abascal attends an event organised by housing activists the day before her scheduled eviction from her home in Madrid.  Photograph: David Canales/SOPA Images/Shutterstock
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, is transported on a stretcher to an ambulance after she was evicted from her Madrid home on Wednesday. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters

blocks.text: Hundreds of people remained camped out in ⁠one of Madrid’s main squares on Tuesday to protest against Maricarmen Abascal’s removal from her home on a stretcher last Wednesday. They are demanding legal reforms including a rent freeze and the ⁠automatic renewal of leases without abusive rent hikes.

It is believed that the first decree has the approval of the conservative Catalan and Basque parties, which previously opposed the government’s housing overhauls, but they are likely to vote down the second decree.
Mónica García, the health minister, celebrated the decision, saying: “We’ve achieved something that even a month ago was unthinkable.”
She added: “It’s time to intervene in the speculative housing market and begin to restore the balance between citizens and vulture funds.”

The Tenants’ Union, which has been the driving force behind the demand for changes to the housing law, as well as the occupation of Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol by protesters in recent days, said it needed to read the small print but opposed the policy of dividing the issue into separate decrees.

“It’s a tactic of tearing something into shreds so that all that’s left are scraps,” said Alicia Del Río, a union spokesperson in Madrid. “The union demands the implementation of the Maricarmen decree in its entirety,” she said, referring to a set of changes drawn up by the union. “They have to accept what people are demanding.”

blocks.caption: Protesters clash with police near the Puerta del Sol encampment in Madrid.  Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Junts, the Catalan pro-independence party that would need to back the decree for it to pass, said on Tuesday it was still far from agreeing to ‌it and wanted protection for small landlords, who make up the vast majority of property owners in Spain.
after newsletter promotion
“Owning two properties isn’t the same as owning entire buildings,” said Míriam Nogueras, Junts’ spokesperson in congress. “But here they’re not making any distinction between the two.”

blocks.caption: Housing rights protesters remain camped at Puerta del Sol in Madrid Photograph: Mario Mor ³N/JNA/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, dismissed the proposals. “The government has created a problem that didn’t exist when it took office,” he said. “A problem that was created over eight years can’t be solved in five minutes.”

Urbagestión, the company whose eviction of Abascal last Wednesday forced the housing crisis to the top of the political agenda, has said Abascal can return to her apartment at a rent that will not exceed 30% of her income. On Tuesday, she accepted the offer and will pay €533 (£457) a month – less than a third of the original demand of €1,650 that had led to her eviction.

blocks.caption: A protester in the encampment at Puerta del Sol. The government has 30 days from the decree’s publication to reach a consensus with allies in congress. Photograph: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Underlining the lack of affordable housing, Ada Colau, a housing activist and a former Barcelona mayor, recently revealed that she has had to move out of her rented apartment after 15 years because it became impossible to pay the rent with a single income since she separated from her husband.

Colau, who renounced most of her mayoral salary during her eight years in office, said the market was geared towards dual incomes, whether couples or people sharing, adding that she had gone to live with a relative.

articles.title: COA flags over P700-M undisbursed fuel subsidy in 2025 audit
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) flagged over P700 million worth of fuel subsidies that were not distributed to beneficiaries in its 2025 annual audit report for the Department of Transportation (DOTr)…

blocks.text: The Commission on Audit (COA) flagged over P700 million worth of fuel subsidies that were not distributed to beneficiaries in its 2025 annual audit report for the Department of Transportation (DOTr) but 70% or P1.9 billion were already distributed.

In a "24 Oras" report by Mariz Umali on Tuesday, of the P709.88 million undisbursed amount, P179.96 million was processed but not credited to the bank accounts of beneficiaries, the majority of whom are tricycle drivers, accounting for P120 million.
COA also flagged P1.589 million in fuel subsidies that were disbursed but rejected due to bank transaction issues, such as incorrect account numbers or mismatched beneficiary names in bank records.
Aside from fuel subsidies, other funds were also reportedly undisbursed, such as those allocated for drivers or operators in Cebu, which was under a state of calamity at the time.
According to the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB), the amount does not represent a single year's funds but rather the combined remaining funds from 2022, 2023, and 2024.

“Bale po, nagkulang po ang benepisyaryo na ibinigay ng DILG. ‘Yung ibang benepisyaryo naman po ng LTFRB, hindi na po mahanap, hindi na po mabigay, kaya po may natira,” LTFRB Acting Chairman Atty. Greg Pua explained.
(The list of beneficiaries provided by the DILG was insufficient. Meanwhile, some of the LTFRB’s beneficiaries could no longer be located or reached, which is why a balance remained.)

“‘Yung 120 million po na sumobra naman po sa sa tricycle, undistributed naman po sa tricycle, dahil naman po ito sa problema sa kanilang account number, sa pangalan. So, hindi po ma-transfer ng LandBank noong panahon na yun,” he added.

(Regarding the excess P120 million intended for tricycle drivers that remained undistributed, this was due to issues with their account numbers or names. Thus, LandBank was unable to process the transfers at the time.)

While COA acknowledged that 70% (P1.9 billion) of the total subsidy allotment was distributed as of November 30, 2025, it stressed that the remaining balance must be promptly delivered to qualified beneficiaries.
The LTFRB stated that legally, the remaining subsidies can no longer be distributed as the funds expire every two years.

“Legally, technically, hindi pwede. Kasi ‘yung pondo ay nag-expire na siya every two years. Kung pwede, palitan na lang namin ‘yung benepisyaryo para maitulong din namin sa mga nangangailangan po ngayon,” Pua said.

(Legally and technically, it is no longer allowed because the funds expire every two years. If permissible, we would prefer to replace the listed beneficiaries so we can assist those currently in need instead.)
Overpayment, Love Bus
The government auditors also flagged P2.853 million in overpayments due to duplicate submissions of the “authority to debit account,” which have yet to be refunded according to the audit report.
The undisbursed funds are not lost but have been returned to the national treasury.

Meanwhile, for the P380 million budget for the Love Bus “Libreng Sakay” (Free Ride) Program, the commission questioned why the Department contracted only one company to operate the route, noting that the program intends to support various bus drivers and operators.
According to the LTFRB, the funds were donated to them by the Office of the President and provided specific requirements.
“Dapat ay electric at dapat po ay PWD (person with disability) friendly. So wala pong ibang nakita except this one,” Pua said.
(The buses had to be electric and PWD-friendly (persons with disabilities). No other provider met these specifications except for this one.) — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Province and feds extending affordable child-care program in Ontario, but fees stay the same
articles.summary: Ontario and the federal government have agreed to extend the national affordable child-care program in the province for another four years, but it may not live up to its signature goal — lowering…

image.caption: While about half of the provinces are offering average fees at $10 a day, Ontario's are an average of $19 a day, capped at $22. (Nathan Denette/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Toronto

Ontario and the federal government have agreed to extend the national affordable child-care program in the province for another four years, but it may not live up to its signature goal — lowering parent fees to an average of $10 a day.
Province's child-care average to stay at $19 a day until June 2027
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 9:51 AM EDT | Last Updated: 15 minutes ago
Feds extend Ontario child-care agreement to 2031

Ontario and the federal government have agreed to extend the national affordable child-care program in the province for another four years, but it comes with no promises of further lowering the fees parents pay.

The province is one of only two, including Alberta, that had not reached longer-term deals beyond the program's initial five years, and securing funding until at least 2031 will give operators and parents some certainty.
But what it may not do is see the program live up to its signature goal — lowering parent fees to an average of $10 a day.

items: Ontario yet to meet $10 a day child-care program goal as waitlists keep growing in Toronto
Ontario should create more child care spaces, instead of focusing on cost alone: expert

blocks.text: While about half of the provinces are offering average fees at that level, Ontario's are an average of $19 a day, capped at $22.
In its new four-year agreement with the federal government, Ontario has committed to maintain fees at that level until June 30, 2027.
What happens after that is still up for discussion.
The agreement provides stability for Ontario parents and child-care operators, federal Jobs and Families Minister Patty Hajdu said.
"Obviously this has been a challenging piece of work, but it's been an amazing piece of work," she said in an interview.
"There are still parents that are saving in Ontario about $9,000 per child, even with the rate being an average of $19."
Waitlists continue to grow: minister

The four-year agreement comes with $12 billion from the federal government, and on top of that Ontario will also get its share of an additional $5.4 billion for the national program that Hajdu announced earlier this year.
The new money addresses Ontario's fiscal hole, at least in the short term, Ontario Education Minister Paul Calandra said.

"[Minister Hajdu] understood that there was a massive shortfall in her program and came back with more money, and this allows us to at least get probably to the end of [2027] with the current fees that we're at," he said in an interview.

"If they want to get down lower, then they're going to have to provide significantly more dollars to do that. But this provides good stability for parents and for the operators. So I'm very happy with what she's been able to accomplish."

items: 5 years on, Ontario says long-term viability of federal daycare program at risk

blocks.text: Hajdu said she has been hearing from parents more on the availability of child care. Waitlists in some regions of Ontario have continued to grow, in some cases by several hundred per cent since before the national program sparked increased demand.
The province was supposed to have created 86,000 affordable spaces by this year under the deal with the federal government, but has so far fallen short at just shy of 60,000.

Calandra said the province continues to work toward that target and expects a good deal of spaces to become available in the next year, as most new schools under construction have child care attached.
Ontario's financial accountability officer has estimated that the demand spurred by lower fees would put the need for new spaces closer to 220,000.

articles.title: UK PM Burnham seeks 'hope again' at Labour Party conference
articles.summary: Andy Burnham is seeking a delicate balance between optimism and realism at Labour's annual party conference. He promised hope and an end to "politics as usual" but also an "honest conversation" about…

image.caption: Andy Burnham evoked surely Labour's most universally popular past government, the post-war adminstration under Clement Atlee, in his speechImage: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

blocks.text: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, only in the role for a few months after replacing Keir Starmer, has told the Labour Party conference in his native Liverpool that his government wants to restore hope and end "politics as usual."

But the UK's seventh prime minister in a decade is trying to balance a series of evidently conflicting fiscal goals: bolstering economic growth, reducing cost-of-living pressures, safeguarding pensions and making care costs more affordable, upgrading creaking infrastructure and significantly boosting military spending.

That's all while battling a populist challenge from Reform UK and Restore Britain on the right and the Green Party on the left. This led Labour to severe local and regional election defeats in May and ultimately spelt his predecessor Starmer's demise.

blocks.caption: Housing Secretary and party members' favorite Angela Rayner was among the speakers warming up the audience on Tuesday ahead of BurnhamImage: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Burnham say in his conference speech?

Burnham, a Liverpool lad who was mayor of Manchester prior to moving to take up Britain's top political job, repeated his most common mantra since coming to power, namely that "more of the same" will not solve the various issues facing the UK.
"We can't carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards," Burnham said. "More of the same isn't good enough and isn't going to get us where we need to be."
The conference's banner headline "hope again" was not incompatible with a more honest conversation, Burnham said.
"Hope comes from honesty ... and saying the things politicians usually avoid," he said.

He cited Labour's post-war government under Clement Atlee, famed for achievements like setting up Britain's National Health Service, as an example of his party past credentials, having "built the peace" in the public interest. He said that since the 1980s and the Conservative-dominated Margaret Thatcher era of his youth, this direction was lost.

"I will say it straight, Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time. Deindustrialization, deregulation, privatization, austerity, Brexit, and what has it given us? A country run for vested interests, not in the public interest — with power held in too few hands, and too many places left to drift," Burnham said.

Burnham told the audience he would take on "the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long," including social care, high levels of youth unemployment, and greater public control of once-nationalized core interests like energy, water and housing.
"The British right talk about 'taking back control," Burnham said, evoking the slogan of the 2016 Brexit campaign. "Never forget that they are the ones who gave it away in the first place!"

blocks.caption: Major UK broadcasters are also on site in Liverpool for Labour's conference week, hoping for face time with the prime minsiter and other leadersImage: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why is Burnham, and Britain, in such a tricky bind?
Burnham said on coming to power that he wanted his premiership to be a "circuit-breaker for Britain" after years of rising prices and anemic growth.

He hit the ground with a handful of new policies like a cap on bus fares, temporarily removing value added tax from electricity bills amid the Iran war, and announcing a bid to stamp out rough sleeping.
But critics say his more grand stated strategy lacks detail and could prove economically unfeasible.

Burnham is constrained by a series of factors, including Labour's 2024 election campaign pledges under Starmer's leadership, Britain's strained public finances, and the suddenly risk-averse debt markets that have started heaping pressure on most developed economies of late.
Borrowing costs for his UK government, as it eyes a series of new banner spending plans, hit a 10-year-high on the morning of Burnham's speech.
In a sign of this lacking spending wiggle room, Burnham has already pushed back his stated aim to formulate reform plans for Britain's social care system.

He said on Tuesday that a "National Care System" would be put forward in time for the next election, currently scheduled for 2029. He said it would be a change "as significant" to the UK as the foundation of the state-funded National Health Service, and also essential to ensure the wider NHS' survival.
He said the plan would be "fully funded, and not by borrowing."

Burnham said that he did not expect such reforms to be easy, and acknowledged "I may pay a political price," but he said they were necessary steps and the kind of leadership he'd promised the party when seeking to replace Starmer this summer.

blocks.caption: Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood addressed the conference on Monday, with the anti-migration Reform UK probably the biggest electoral threat to Labour — if not necessarily the party Labour voters are migratingImage: Gary Roberts/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: These challenging economic realities coincide with Labour facing multi-pronged political threats. articles.title: North Korea has recently completed two road bridges easing transport to strategic allies Russia and China
articles.summary: Two recently opened bridges are expected to ease trade and transport between North Korea and its powerful neighbors. The new connections come as Pyongyang builds strategic ties with China and Russia.

image.caption: Stretching 3 kilometers, the New Yalu River bridge can carry more traffic and ease trade Image: Kyodo News/IMAGO

blocks.text: A long-delayed bridge linking North Korea and China could finally open in early October, more than a decade after its completion, as Pyongyang simultaneously expands transport links with Russia.

South Korean news outlets have reported that the New Yalu River Bridge, connecting China's northeastern city of Dandong with the trade hub of Sinuiju in northwestern North Korea, could formally open by October 6, which marks the 77th anniversary of North Korea-China diplomatic relations.

Analysis published by the 38 North think tank showed significant progress on customs, immigration and warehouse facilities on the North Korean side, where construction had remained largely unfinished for years.
The cable-stayed New Yalu River Bridge is located about 15 kilometers (9 miles) downstream toward the Yellow Sea from the older crossings connecting central Dandong and Sinuiju.
The four-lane road bridge stretches over 3,000 meters across the river, with a network of approach roads connecting it to the surrounding areas.

It was intended to ease pressure on the aging Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which carries both road and rail traffic and remains one of the most important routes between North Korea and China, Pyongyang's top trading partner.
Improving links to both Russia and China

The expected opening of the improved link with China comes after a road bridge crossing the Tumen River located across the peninsula was opened on September 7 connecting North Korea's Rason region with Khasan in Russia's Primorsky region.
Until then, the two countries' narrow land border had been connected by rail but not by road.

"North Korea allowed the Chinese bridge to sit unused for more than a decade, but North Korea hurried more than Russia did," Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW.

That difference, he argues, provides clues to Pyongyang's strategy, which appears to be deliberately managing the pace of its improving relations with Russia and China to avoid returning to excessive dependence on Beijing.

"If it depends too much on China as it did in the past, North Korea's autonomy could be undermined," Han said, adding that Pyongyang is seeking to take advantage of good ties with both China and Russia while preserving its independence.

The former Unification Ministry official added that Russia has an interest in expanding transport routes through North Korea toward the Pacific, including through the port of Rajin, while Pyongyang could benefit from increased trade, tourism and opportunities to send workers to Russia.
He added that Russia needs North Korean labor, arguing that North Korean workers are more diligent than their Russian counterparts.
China, meanwhile, has its own reasons to ensure that North Korea does not become excessively reliant on Russia, the former official said.
"From China's perspective, it needs to keep North Korea from leaning too far toward Russia," Han said.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have grown since 2023, when North Korea began providing weapons and troops for the Ukraine war. As the Russia-North Korea strategic relationship has deepened, China has been taking steps to reassert itself as the North's primary partner.
Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said the bridges have added geopolitical implications.

"Pyongyang could now use its deepening ties with China and Russia, along with Trump's interest in engaging Kim, to strengthen its diplomatic leverage and take a more assertive approach toward South Korea," Ahn told DW.
North Korea slowly reopens
Pyongyang virtually sealed its borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, sharply reducing trade and restricting even the entry of foreign diplomats.

Cross-border freight trains between Dandong and Sinuiju resumed in 2022. Passenger trains followed on March 12 this year, restoring rail travel between North Korea and China for the first time in six years.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine
Ahn described the prospective bridge opening as historically significant.
"The New Yalu River Bridge is effectively the first modern bridge between North Korea and China," Ahn said.
Plans for a new bridge date to 2009, when then-Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and North Korean officialsagreed on the project to relieve the Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, built in 1943.

Construction on the new bridge began in 2011, largely financed by Beijing, and the bridge itself was essentially completed in 2014. The opening was complicated by delays on building a customs center on the North Korean side.
Ahn added the opening could be interpreted as a signal that Pyongyang intends to move toward greater economic openness, even if that process proceeds slowly.
Yalu River Bridge to bolster China trade
A former senior South Korean Unification Ministry official, who requested anonymity, told DW that renewed trade could also benefit China's northeastern provinces of Liaoning, Jilin and Heilongjiang.
Before sanctions and the pandemic disrupted commerce, businesses in the region imported North Korean goods, including seafood, while Chinese products flowed in the opposite direction.
"Both sides need this," the former official said.
North Korea needs Chinese goods and opportunities to earn foreign currency, while parts of northeastern China can benefit from renewed cross-border commerce, he added.
The official said the long delay also reflected Pyongyang's previous reluctance to build customs, logistics and other infrastructure required on its side.

blocks.caption: The bridge itself was completed several years ago, but its opening has been delayedImage: Yomiuri Shimbun/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The fact that it is opening now means North Korea has built customs, clearance facilities and logistics warehouses," he said. "From that perspective, North Korea needs it more. It now needs goods coming in from China."
Former South Korean intelligence official Han expects the new crossing to accelerate trade recovery toward pre-pandemic trade levels.
"The opening of the Yalu River bridge will further stimulate trade between North Korea and China," Han told DW.
North Korea particularly needs imports for construction and industrial production, including factory components, he said.
But Han cautioned against expecting an uncontrolled trade boom.

He pointed to Pyongyang's increasingly centralized trade system, under which the state has tightened control over imports instead of allowing individual factories and enterprises to conduct commerce more independently.
A shortage of foreign currency could provide another constraint, Han said, pointing to the sharp rise in the unofficial exchange rate for the US dollar inside North Korea.

articles.title: Women and children displaced by Nepal's floods say safe housing, privacy and stability remain out of reach
articles.summary: Families living in temporary shelters in northern Nepal say safety and privacy remain out of reach as concerns about trafficking and abuse mount.

image.caption: Uncertainty over permanent housing and livelihoods is putting girls at risk, says Save the ChildrenImage: Prakash Mathema/AFP

blocks.text: One month after deadly flash floods in Nepal swept away Karishma Tamang's community in Rasuwa District, the pregnant 26-year-old is still struggling to find a safe place to call home.

Karishma, who is expecting her second child, has been moving from place to place with her 4-year-old daughter since the devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border at the end of August.
"Initially, we were kept in a covered hall at Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District," she told DW, adding that hundreds of people shared the same shelter for days.

"Now we have shifted to a small makeshift family tent at the nearby Barahachaur area. Still, we can't sleep during rainy nights as it leaks when it rains." Her brother and his two children remain missing after the flood.

blocks.caption: Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environmentImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: There is no proper toilet, although a small makeshift latrine has been set up near the tents, Karishma said.
Children and pregnant women like Karishma need privacy and safety, but such facilities remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areas.
"It would be great to have a stable place to stay, where I could cook my own meals, feel safe and have some comfort," she said.
Safety concerns in temporary shelters

The August 26 flood, triggered by a glacier collapse along the Nepal-China border, killed about 1,450 people and left more than 5,500 missing. Reconstruction costs are estimated to be $4.8 billion (€4.2 billion).

At least seven people, including girls, women and local volunteers at temporary shelters and camps, spoke to DW. Although none reported experiencing sexual harassment or abuse, their accounts point to widespread concerns about safety and vulnerability in the aftermath of the floods.

Sabita Tamang, who lost her 5-year-old daughter, nephew and niece in the floods, is also staying in a makeshift tent in Barahachaur. The 24-year-old said she has to travel beyond the nearest tap to bathe and collect water.

blocks.caption: Privacy and safety remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areasImage: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We feel uncomfortable taking a bath in an open space among strangers and unknown locals," she told DW. "Many children have seen their family members, friends and neighbors caught in the floods," she said, raising concerns about the impact on their mental health and education.
Risk of trafficking and abuse

Save the Children Nepal has warned that protection measures for children and their families must be strengthened across flood-affected areas amid concerns about trafficking, violence, exploitation and child marriage.
Many families have moved into rented rooms. Yet hundreds are being housed in temporary shelters and makeshift tents in Nuwakot and Dhading districts.
Save the Children Nepal raised concerns about privacy and safety for girls and women because unfamiliar people have unrestricted access to shared spaces.

Ayush Joshi, director for advocacy, campaigns, communications and media at Save the Children Nepal, told DW that the organization's report was based on qualitative assessments involving affected people, including women and children, as well as volunteers deployed in flood-hit areas.

blocks.caption: The disaster has affected more than 80,000 people. Thousands who lost everything are living in emergency sheltersImage: Pedro Pardo/AFP

blocks.text: "Many temporary shelters are built without planning. Camps on the outskirts of towns have inadequate lighting at night and lack separate washrooms and private spaces," Joshi told DW, noting that there is unrestricted access for unfamiliar people.
"Such situations naturally increase the risk of insecurity, potential harassment and exploitation, especially for young girls and children."

According to Joshi, in the aftermath of the disaster, many people became separated from their families, while some children lost their lives and older siblings had to become caregivers for younger siblings.

"In such circumstances, cases of school dropouts and child marriage could increase," he added, referring to Save the Children's field assessment. "We have seen many children facing mental health issues, like becoming angry, frightened and crying loudly. There is a need for socio-emotional healing."
What does the government say?

The Nepali government has also assessed the risks of trafficking and potential child abuse and has collaborated with organizations such as Save the Children, the police and local authorities to strengthen protection measures at displacement sites.
After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes

Chakra Bahadur Budha, spokesperson at the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, said the government had increased monitoring and surveillance and was raising awareness about gender-based violence and trafficking.
"We have mobilized and kept all relevant stakeholders on high alert to check at points of entry and exit, so as to protect affected people from being trafficked or abused," he told DW.

Authorities took back at least 78 children from two Buddhist monasteries in Kathmandu and placed them in temporary camps. Budha explained that the monasteries had rescued and supported the children, offering long-term shelter, education and employment, but the government discourages such arrangements outside established procedures.

"We have strictly discouraged religious or charitable organizations from keeping children without following legal procedures," Budha told DW. "Adoption has also been discouraged for now, but children can be placed with close relatives, such as uncles and aunts, for their protection after verification of their relationship."
The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said at least 541 children have either lost their parents or become separated from their families.
Initial assessments indicate that learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning centers in flood-affected areas in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts.

articles.title: Estonia blames Russia for arson at defence company supplying Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia has been accused of launching sabotage attacks across a number of European Nato countries which have been helping Ukraine.

blocks.text: Russia was behind an arson attack on an Estonian defence company in the capital Tallinn last month, authorities say.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the attack on Milrem Robotics - which supplies Ukraine with unmanned military vehicles - was ordered by Russian special services, but gave no details.
Moscow has been accused of launching sabotage attacks in a number of Nato countries that have been helping Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February 2022.

Russia denies such allegations and has been quick to reject the Estonian accusation, too. But EU countries have rushed to Estonia's support, adding such attacks will not deter them from helping Ukraine.
The attack on Milrem Robotics occurred on the night of 14-15 August.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said that, based on information collected by the country's Internal Security Service, "we can conclude with certainty that the arson attack... was an act of sabotage ordered by the special services of the Russian Federation".

Security service chief Margo Palloson told broadcaster ERR that Russia was "constantly planning, looking for opportunities, trying to find people who would carry out attacks", but that last month's arson attack was its first successful attack this year.

The foreign minister said the perpetrators had been arrested and Palloson said they were Latvians who had been living in Russia and taken part in previous attacks. Three suspects were arrested in Latvia and extradited to Estonia earlier this month.
Margus Tsahkna said that "this act of sabotage is part of Russia's broader campaign across Europe, aimed at intimidating us and weakening our support for Ukraine".

French President Emmanuel Macron responded to Estonia's assessment, saying "the multiplication of these hostile acts represents a dangerous escalation by Russia, which will only lead it into a dead end".
He mentioned the incident at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, in which an explosive-laden drone was found near Ukrainian cargo planes.
"Russia needs to know that it will not overcome our unity or our determination to continue supporting Ukraine," Macron added.
An EU spokesman said the 27-member bloc would not cease supporting Ukraine.
Nato chief Mark Rutte urged European governments to stay calm and continue supporting Ukraine.

"Russia continues its reckless campaign of hostile actions against Nato allies. It is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine. But Russia is failing. It is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine and it is failing to undermine our unity and support for Ukraine," Rutte said.

In August alone, Russia was either accused or suspected of the Leipzig airport attack in Germany, a major fire at a warehouse of a defence firm in Bulgaria, a large explosion at a munitions factory outside Rome in Italy, an attempted arson attack on a Ukrainian-owned drone manufacturer in Slovakia, and two suspicious fires in Poland - the latest in a country which has reported several such attacks.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms that tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
Estonia's internal security service, known as Kapo, said Russia was continuing to look for further opportunities for either sabotage or other hostile acts.

"Individuals recruited for such operations may be misled or manipulated and may be given false or fabricated justifications for their actions in an effort to conceal the involvement of the Russian state," Kapo head Palloson said, external.
Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman said "such statements are baseless, ill-considered, have absolutely no relation to reality, and lack any form of reasoning".
"We cannot and will not take such statements seriously," Dmitry Peskov said.

articles.title: Man charged over AI image of crocodile in Singapore reservoir
articles.summary: The defendant could face jail or a fine after the image sparked a search operation in the city’s largest reservoir.

blocks.text: The national water agency said it was alerted to a crocodile sighting in Pandan Reservoir on 20 August. Agency officials and national parks staff conducted search and capture operations in the area. The Singapore Rowing Association and Singapore Canoe Federation were told the suspend their activities.
But the following day, the water agency confirmed that the crocodile image was fake and reported it to the police.
The case will return to court in November and Ye Lin could face a prison sentence and a large fine if he is found guilty.

In Singapore, sending a false message is punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to S$10,000 (about US$7,800; £5,900), or both. Obstructing justice carries up to seven years in prison, a fine, or both.
Police allege that Ye Lin created the photo of the crocodile using artificial intelligence before sending it to a colleague.
"The man subsequently deleted the image and the related application in an attempt to conceal his actions," the police statement said.
It is not clear how the national water agency was notified of the false photo that Ye Lin sent to his colleague.

articles.title: Marcoleta camp maintains P75M was 'campaign contribution'
articles.summary: Senator Rodante Marcoleta"s defense team maintained that the money he admitted to receiving was part of his campaign contributions, but the prosecution argued that the lawmaker paid a tax that…

blocks.text: Published September 29, 2026 8:57pm

Senator Rodante Marcoleta’s defense team maintained that the money he admitted to receiving was part of his campaign contributions, but the prosecution argued that the lawmaker paid a tax that suggested otherwise.

In a 24 Oras report from Maki Pulido on Tuesday, the Sandiganbayan First Division held its first trial day for the case of Marcoleta, who is accused of violating Presidential Decree 46, which prohibits government officials from receiving monetary gifts.
The prosecution presented Attorney Victoria Besinio of the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) Political Finance Affairs Department as a witness.
During the questioning of Marcoleta’s lawyer, the COMELEC determined that the money given to Marcoleta was a campaign contribution.
However, the prosecution argued that Marcoleta’s camp also submitted to the COMELEC proof that they paid donor’s tax.
It could not be treated as a campaign donation because campaign donations are not taxable, the prosecution argued.
Marcoleta had publicly stated on a television program that he received P75 million in campaign donations, which he did not state on his Statement of Contribution and Expenditures.
The prosecution used this statement as evidence during the trial.

While Marcoleta did not state who gave him this money, he would later name former House lawmaker Mike Defensor and Joseph Espiritu as donors in a verified position paper. Both Defensor and Espiritu are his co-accused in the case.
